subject: Routing throttle & temporary SLO exception request
messages:
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>
To: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Priya Rao <prao@checkoutly.com>, accounts@checkoutly.com
Date: 2027-11-14T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: [ALERT] Latency surge affecting Checkoutly — initial report

Team / Priya,

Quick heads-up: starting ~08:50 PT we observed a spike in 99th percentile latency for gen-api requests routed to us-east-1 serving the Checkoutly tenant. Impact: elevated p99 to ~1.4s (baseline ~420ms) and an increase in tail error rates tied to request timeouts before retries. Throughput has remained steady, but the backlog on worker queues has grown — continuous batching windows are lengthening and KV cache hit ratio has dropped for the last 20 minutes.

What I've attached: a short diagnostic snapshot (diagnostic_snapshot_20271114.txt) and the qcache dump (qcache_stats_20271114.csv). Early hypothesis: an interaction between recent routing changes (sticky routing for regional affinity) and a hot-shard pattern in the KV cache for that customer.

Immediate asks:
- Eng/SRE: can we confirm whether the routing change caused uneven partitioning (karthik, ben)? If hot-shard, we should consider temporary traffic rebalancing or a thin throttle by route.
- Product: we need a quick decision on whether to accept a temporary SLO exception for Checkoutly (p99/SLO) while we mitigate. Marissa / Evelyn, is that acceptable and what wording we want to give them?
- CS (Evelyn): start drafting a customer-facing note; keep it succinct and set expectations.

If routing rebalancing is non-trivial, my fallback recommendation is a short, targeted routing throttle for Checkoutly's highest-QPS keyspace for 30–60m to allow cache warmup and to reduce queueing. That would likely keep median latency stable while bringing p99 back down. Downsides: small increase in tail errors and potential tokenization backpressure.

I'll keep collecting traces; assigning JIRA-RI-3472.

— Soojin
SRE
Redwood Inference

Attachments: diagnostic_snapshot_20271114.txt (text), qcache_stats_20271114.csv (csv)
From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Priya Rao <prao@checkoutly.com>, accounts@checkoutly.com
Date: 2027-11-14T10:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: [ALERT] Latency surge affecting Checkoutly — initial report

Thanks Soojin — good triage. A few product-level constraints to keep in mind before we decide on throttles or SLO exceptions:

1) Commercial/contract: Checkoutly has a p99 SLA in their enterprise addendum. Any formal SLO exception needs legal + sales signoff but we can push a temporary customer notice while we sort signoff.
2) UX: we prefer short, controlled throttles to a full-tenant routing diversion — customers tolerate brief throttles better when framed as a protective measure.
3) Risk/cost tradeoff: if quantization or a reduced model variant can restore latency without heavy routing changes, that would be preferable, but it may affect quality.

My asks:
- Karthik/Ben: can you evaluate two options and share a short impact matrix within 90 minutes?
  A) targeted routing throttle (as Soojin suggested): estimated customer-visible error increase, duration, rollback steps.
  B) partial quantization profile rollback / serve from non-quantized variant for Checkoutly traffic: expected latency improvement, quality delta (if you have quick eval), and effort to switch back.
- Soojin: prepare the customer-facing one-paragraph notice draft (I started a file — see attached cust_notice_draft_20271114.txt). Keep it factual, avoid technical jargon; we'll iterate and send after internal approvals.

Priya / accounts: we will share a short note in the next 2–3 hours and follow up with a more detailed RCA. Appreciate patience — we are treating this as high priority.

— Evelyn
Director, Customer Success
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: [ALERT] Latency surge affecting Checkoutly — initial report

Quick technical readout (summary) — ran targeted queries against the qcache dump and trace aggregates.

Root cause hypothesis: the recent sticky-routing patch resulted in an uneven distribution of user keys that fell disproportionately into a small set of inference shards for Checkoutly. Those shards are now seeing a hot prefix pattern which both increases KV lookup times (cache eviction pressure) and lengthens batching windows.

Option A — routing throttle (low risk, low code):
- Mechanism: apply a rate cap at the routing layer for the offending keyspace (we can do per-tenant caps today).
- Impact: expected p99 reduction to ~550–700ms within 10–20 minutes as queues drain; some requests will be delayed or receive a 429 which our client SDK retries gracefully.
- Rollback: remove cap; immediate rebalancing may reintroduce pressure.
- Ops effort: ~15–25m to enable + monitor.

Option B — partial quantization rollback / non-quant variant (higher risk to quality):
- Mechanism: route Checkoutly traffic to the non-quantized model variant for the affected endpoints or apply the higher-precision quant profile.
- Impact: expected p99 improvement comparable to throttle (~500–650ms) and preserves success rates, but may increase inference cost ~12–18% while active. Quality delta: minimal for embeddings and classification; generative outputs may have marginal improvements.
- Rollback: switch mapping back to quantized variant.
- Ops effort: ~30–45m (we have automated mapping toggles but need canary + smoke-tests).

Recommendation: start with Option A (routing throttle) immediately to protect SLOs while we stage Option B as a lower-latency, customer-friendly follow-up if cost/quality tradeoffs are acceptable. We'll instrument a quick manual canary for Option B while throttle is active.

I'll stand by to implement Option A if you authorize. Link to internal play: https://drive.redwood/team/sre/incident-20271114-decomp-notes (contains rollout snippets and the JIRA ticket).

— Karthik
Staff Engineer, Runtime
Redwood Inference
